# Storyboard — every beat, every section

**Generated by `npm run board`. Do not edit by hand.**

A hand-written board drifts from the code within a day, and then two
documents disagree about what the video is. This one is read out of each
section's `beats.ts`, so the board and the build are the same fact.

Spine: `storyboard/STORY_SPINE.md` · Gates: `skills/STORY_STRUCTURE.md`
Chain check: `npm run check:chain` · Frames: `npm run frames:all`

## Section 03 — From an ID to a meaning

`13` beats · `1:49` · script: `video-script/03-from-an-id-to-a-meaning.md` · route: `/section-03`

- **Enters on** — a row number has no meaning in it. So how does it know what anything means?

| # | id | s | rel | Beat | Voice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `how-it-gets-meaning` | 6 | want | `4021` alone; a table edge rises into frame | Here’s how it gets meaning out of a row number. |
| 2 | `the-model-has-a-table` | 10 | so | We back away; the table runs past the top of frame | The model has a table. One row for every token in that list — all hundred and fifty-four thousand of them. |
| 3 | `which-row-to-fetch` | 5 | so | The number travels up the table to its own row | The ID is just which row to go and fetch. |
| 4 | `this-row` | 6 | so | That row slides out of the table and comes forward | So token four thousand and twenty-one pulls out this row. |
| 5 | `four-thousand-and-ninety-six` | 8 | and-yet | The row extends sideways past both edges of frame | Four thousand and ninety-six numbers. For one small piece of text. |
| 6 | `called-an-embedding` | 9 | so | The row holds; a label lands on it | This row is called an embedding. And it’s the first thing in the whole machine that actually means something. |
| 7 | `dog-and-cat` | 8 | so | Two more rows slide out and stack under it | Here’s why it means something. Let’s pull out "dog", and "cat". |
| 8 | `close-but-not-the-same` | 8 | so | The two rows align; the values that nearly match light up | They’re not the same — but they’re close. Lots of these numbers nearly match. |
| 9 | `now-tuesday` | 6 | wall | A third row aligns; almost nothing lights | Now "Tuesday". Not close to either of them. |
| 10 | `training-did-it` | 11 | so | The three rows fold into three points, spaced by likeness | Nobody sat down and made that happen. Training did it. Words that get used in similar ways ended up with similar rows. |
| 11 | `where-the-row-sits` | 10 | and-yet | The points hold; a brace measures the two distances | So the meaning isn’t in any one number. It’s in where the row sits relative to all the other rows. |
| 12 | `this-is-what-goes-in` | 6 | therefore | The points unfold back into the `dog` row, alone | And that’s what goes into the model. Not "dog". This. |
| 13 | `same-word-same-row` | 16 | and-yet | The same row is pulled twice more; all three are identical | But here’s the thing to hold on to. This row is stored in a table. Which means it is exactly the same every single time the word "dog" turns up. Same word, same row, always. |

## Section 04 — The word looks around

`13` beats · `1:40` · script: `video-script/04-the-word-looks-around.md` · route: `/section-04`

- **Enters on** — that row is the same every single time. So how does the word ever mean two things?

| # | id | s | rel | Beat | Voice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `starts-out-identical` | 8 | want | The three identical rows collapse into one | So every "dog" starts out identical. Which can’t be right — and it isn’t, for long. |
| 2 | `never-on-its-own` | 6 | so | We back off; every token’s row is there, in a line | Because a token never stays on its own. It’s sitting in a sentence. |
| 3 | `every-token-looks` | 6 | so | Our row lifts slightly out of the line | And before anything else happens, every token gets to look at the others. |
| 4 | `how-much-do-you-matter` | 9 | so | Lines shoot from our row to every other row | Here’s what looking means. Our token asks every other token one question: how much do you matter to me? |
| 5 | `some-matter-a-lot` | 6 | so | The lines thicken and thin | Some matter a lot. Most barely matter at all. |
| 6 | `only-backwards` | 7 | wall | The lines running forward fade out and go | And it can only look backwards — at the words already there. Not at what’s coming. |
| 7 | `mixes-it-in` | 8 | so | Material travels along the surviving lines into our row | Then it takes a bit of each one, in proportion, and mixes it into itself. |
| 8 | `and-its-row-changes` | 6 | and-yet | Our row’s values visibly change where the flow landed | And its row changes. Same token. New numbers. |
| 9 | `thats-attention` | 8 | so | The lines withdraw; a label lands | That’s attention. That’s the whole idea — every token adjusting itself based on the company it’s in. |
| 10 | `two-sentences` | 8 | so | The sentence slides left; a second assembles beside it | Now watch why that matters. "The dog barked." And "a hot dog." |
| 11 | `nothing-like-each-other` | 9 | wall | Both `dog` rows lift out and align — clearly different | Same word both times. Started as the exact same row. Ended up nothing like each other. |
| 12 | `the-word-in-this-sentence` | 9 | therefore | The row they started from ghosts in behind both, identical | So the numbers don’t belong to the word any more. They belong to the word in this sentence. |
| 13 | `could-not-have-known` | 10 | and-yet | The ghost fades; the two rows hold apart | And notice — none of that could have been worked out ahead of time. It depends entirely on what you typed. |

| 5 | `no-french-expert` | 13 | wall | It drops back; no labels appear on any of them | Nobody assigned them subjects. There’s no French expert, no maths expert. They’re just two hundred and eighty-eight different blocks that came out of training different from each other. |

| 5 | `quite-often-the-same` | 7 | so | The repeating blocks stay in the box instead of returning | The next token quite often wants some of the same experts the last one did. |
| 6 | `only-fetch-the-misses` | 13 | so | The next word’s fetches split: most from the box, a few from the drive | So you don’t fetch every time. You keep the ones that keep coming back in fast memory, and you only go to the drive for the ones you’re missing. |

## Section 13 — What that number actually bought

`12` beats · `1:54` · script: `video-script/13-what-that-number-bought.md` · route: `/section-13`

- **Enters on** — it's a price, not a wall. So what did "18 billion active" actually get us?
- **Exits on** — (none — the thesis lands)

| # | id | s | rel | Beat | Voice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `eighteen-billion-active` | 4 | want | The plan dissolves; `18` rises and holds alone | So. Eighteen billion active. |
| 2 | `what-that-number-tells-you` | 5 | so | We slide back to the opening: the number, and the block behind it | Here’s what that number is actually telling you. |
| 3 | `that-part-is-true` | 16 | so | A small work bar draws itself beside it | Per word, this thing does the thinking of a model about a twentieth of its size. That’s real. That’s why it’s quick, and why it’s cheap to run per word. That part is completely true. |
| 4 | `all-of-it-in-reach` | 11 | wall | The block returns behind it, whole, and settles heavily | But all of it still has to be within reach. Because it never knows which part it wants until the moment it wants it. |
| 5 | `a-compute-number` | 8 | therefore | A label lands between the bar and the block | So: "active parameters" is a compute number. It was never a memory number. |
| 6 | `compute-not-memory` | 8 | therefore | The bar and the block separate into two labelled halves | Sparse routing buys you compute. It doesn’t buy you memory. |
| 7 | `one-chip-or-four` | 15 | and-yet | A second card slides in beside the first; chips stack under each | And here’s the part I didn’t expect. This model has a hundred and twenty billion parameters, and it fits on one chip. This one has three hundred and twenty, and needs four. |
| 8 | `about-five-percent-both` | 6 | and-yet | Both cards light their active share; the two shares match | Both of them use about five percent of themselves to answer you. |
| 9 | `chopped-finer` | 7 | so | Each card’s block divides — one coarse, one into many fine pieces | The difference is that this one is chopped finer. More experts, smaller each. |
| 10 | `better-and-harder` | 8 | and-yet | The fine-grained one’s chips grow while its pieces get smaller | Which is exactly why it’s better — and exactly why it’s harder to hold. |
| 11 | `the-trend` | 10 | therefore | The second card withdraws; ours holds with its four chips | So the better these models get at using less of themselves, the more of them you have to keep lying around. |
| 12 | `cheap-to-run-not-small` | 16 | therefore | Everything clears to one card | A three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter model doing eighteen billion of work is still a three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter model. It just isn’t a three-hundred-and-twenty-billion-parameter bill. And that’s the difference between something that’s cheap to run — and something that’s small. |
